# Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Sampling

Also called: Hierarchical Sampling, Two-Stage Sampling, Coarse-Fine NeRF

## Overview
Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Sampling is a strategy that improves the learning of high-frequency details in Neural Radiance Fields by decoupling the search for opaque regions from their detailed reconstruction [S1, S4, unofficial]. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling, which wastes computation on empty space and misses fine structures, by first using a coarse network to identify where the scene is opaque and then clustering a second set of samples around those opaque locations to train a fine network [S1, S4, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from standard uniform sampling by adaptively concentrating samples based on learned opacity, and from its sibling [TermiNeRF](8828-terminerf.md) by not explicitly modeling the termination of rays but rather refining the density estimation within the sampled intervals [S4, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The family relies on a two-stage evaluation pipeline. First, a **coarse network** ($\text{MLP}_{coarse}$) is queried with a set of uniformly distributed samples along the ray to estimate volume density $\sigma$ and color. These samples are typically stratified to reduce aliasing [S4, unofficial]. Second, the rendering weights $w$ derived from the coarse pass serve as a probability density function (PDF) to generate a second set of **fine samples** via inverse transform sampling [S4, unofficial].

The fine network ($\text{MLP}_{fine}$) is then queried on the union of the coarse and fine sample depths, sorted by distance [S4, S5, unofficial]. The final color is computed using standard volume rendering integration over this combined set [S5, unofficial].

A critical implementation constraint is the **gradient flow**. The sampling step is non-differentiable. Gradients must not flow back through the hierarchical sampling logic to the coarse model's density predictions. This is achieved by detaching the coarse samples and weights before passing them to the fine sampling logic [S4, S5, unofficial]. The coarse-to-fine edge must be cut to prevent cyclic definitions in the compute graph [S5, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Coarse-to-Fine NeRF](3406-coarse-to-fine-nerf.md)
The canonical implementation using a coarse MLP to guide uniform-to-importance sampling. It sets itself apart by using fixed heuristics for the coarse-to-fine transition rather than learning the distribution directly.

### [TermiNeRF](8828-terminerf.md)
Splits the NeRF into a sampling network and a shading network. It sets itself apart by learning a direct mapping from camera rays to ideal sampling distributions rather than relying on hierarchical coarse-to-fine depth estimation.

### [NeRF-ID](8867-nerf-id.md)
Replaces heuristic sampling with a differentiable 'proposer' module. It sets itself apart by learning the sampling distribution directly from data, enabling end-to-end training of the coarse network, proposer, and fine network.

## Background
The method was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in the original NeRF paper (2020) [S4, unofficial]. It addresses the limitation that standard coarse-to-fine approaches rely on handcrafted probability density functions rather than being optimized for the specific task [S1, unofficial]. It is widely used in Neural Radiance Field training to balance rendering quality and computational cost.
